title: Officers, civilian employee recognized for dedication to careers
subtitle: None
article: Since 1974, Olga Skinner has worked with police officers.

The Corner Brook woman stood among some of those same police officers once again as she was recognized for her long service during a ceremony which also honoured several local members of the Royal Newfoundland Constabulary for outstanding service during their lengthy careers.

Skinner, who worked with the Department of Social Services in Corner Brook from 1969-74, moved into the Department of Justice in 1974 and worked with the Royal Canadian Mounted Police in Corner Brook until her job was transferred to the RNC, which began servicing Corner Brook in July 1986.
Skinner, who received her long service certificate from Justice Minister Felix Collins Wednesday afternoon, still works in the RNC administration office.

"I've just gone to work everyday and that's it," she said humbly after Wednesday's ceremony. "I guess it's a lot for someone to do something for 40 years, but for me it's been easy and I've enjoyed it."
Still, it was an honour to be recognized during the same event which decorated officers she's worked with for years.
"It's a special moment and they are a great bunch of people to work with," she said.
One officer, Sgt. Greg Poole, who has also worked with the RNC in Northeast Avalon and Labrador West, received a 30 Years Service Bar.

Five other officers received 20 Years Service Medals. They included Sgt. Everett Ogden and Const. John Goss, who have been with the RNC since 1986; Sgt. Richard Wheeler and Const. Brad Saint, who became RNC officers in 1987; and Const. Sharon Smith, who has been with the force since 1989.

Ogden, who was one of the original officers stationed in Corner Brook in 1986, plans to retire from his native city in a few years. Ogden said one of the highlights of his career has been the opportunity to get involved with the community.
He is a member of the RNC's honour guard which participates in city parades and is also an organizer and performer at the RNC's annual dances for seniors.
"That sort of thing is very important to me because that's a part of policing, especially community policing," said Ogden.
"I take great pride in that. It's important that some of us do take the bull by the horns to do good and do extra work above and beyond."

The Police Exemplary Service Medals are not just a recognition of longtime service, but are presented to officers who characterize good conduct and whose performance has been deemed worthy of recognition. The medals were presented by Lt.-Gov. John Crosbie.
"Whenever I think of the police force, I think of peace, order and good government, which is a very important part of the constitution of Canada," said Crosbie.

"You can't have peace, order and good government unless you have an effective, efficient, competent and well-trained police force, which we are lucky to have today with the Royal Newfoundland Constabulary and the RCMP."

Seven other officers, meanwhile, were presented with supervisor leadership program certificates from Memorial University. They included Staff Sgt. Roy Elliott, Sgt. George Pauls, Sgt. Craig Pilgrim and Sgt. Richard Wheeler from Corner Brook; Sgt. Nolan Norman and Sgt. John Whelan from Labrador West; and Sgt. Terry Hawco from Churchill Falls.
